Thus Angulo., having obtained to less than twenty victories, was aa often saluted with the title emperor. and Titus was denominated emperor by Ilia aomy after the reduction of Jtrusalem. Afterwardn, it came to denominate an absolute monarch or aupreine coinnaander Of an empire. In this senile Joints Cour war called enifferor the same title descended with the dignity to Octavio., Tiberius, and Caligula; and afterwards it became elective., The title emperor does not, and cannot, add anything to I the right* of sovereignly its effect has only been to give precedence and pre-eminence above other eovereigna. It has , been sonietimes disputed, if emperors have the power of diapoeing of the regal title. They have certainly some- times taken upon them to erect kingdoms: thus Bohemia and Poland are said to have been raised to that dignity thus aleo, the emperor Charles 11., in 877, gave Provence to , &eon, putting the diadem on hi. bead, and decreeing him to be called king, on more priscorom imperatorton regibus videretur dominari. And the emperor Leopold erected ducal , Prussia into a kingdom in favour of the elector of Broaden- , burg ; though several of the king. of Huron. refueed to ac- knowledge him in that capacity until the treaty of Utrecht in 1712. In the east, the title and quality of emperor are more frequent than among as: floe., the sovereign princes of China, Japan, Mogul, Persia, h., have been called em- perors. In 1723 the mar of Musoavy assunkd the title of emperor of all the Russian, and procured himself to be recog- nised as such by the prince. and states of Europe. In the wen, the tide was lung restrained to the emperors of Ger- many. The first who bore it was Charlemagne, who had it pmferred upon him by pope Leo fli. having indeed had all the power before. r be imperial prerogatives were formerly wry catenates. At the close of the bacon race, A.D. 1024, they exercised the right of conferring ecclesiastical benefices In Germany ; of receiving the revenue* of them during a vacancy ; of eucceeding to the effecta of intestate ecclesias- tic.; of confirming or annulling the election. of the popm; of aseembling council., and of appointing them to decide concerning the affairs of the church ; of conferring the title of king on their vassils; of granting vacant fiefs ; of re- Paving the revenues of the empire ; of governing Italy Mc its proper sovereigns ol erecting free cities, and of estab- Robing fairs in Heel ; of aseetnbling the diets of the empire, and of Axing the time of their duration ; of coining money, and conferring the same privilege on the states of the em- pire ; and of adminintering both high and low justice within the territoriea of the different nate.. but in the, year 1437 they were reduced to theight of conferring all dignities and titles, except the privilege of heiog a state of the empire ; of preces primaries, or of appointing once during their reign a dignitary in mch chapter or religious house ; of granting diepenrations with respect toll,, age of majority: of erecting cities, aml conferring the privilege of coining money; of calling tlie ineetings of the diet and presiding in them. To which some have added, I. That all the ; /nines and states of Germany were obliged to do them homage, and ,wear fidelity to them. 2. That then or their generals had right to command the forcm of all the princes of the em- pire, when united together, to. The kings of France were anciently also called emperors, at the time when they reigned with their sons, whom they asaociated to the crown. Thus Hugh Capef, having associated hia son Robert, took the title of emperor, Robert that of king ; under which titles they are , mentioned in the History of the Council of Rheims, by Graben, dic. King Robert is also called emperor of the French by Helgau of Fleury. Lewis the Gram upon as.- Paling his son, did the same. J. 111.68 SIVOIM AT Fnonswan.—Cla Wednesday evening a concert of sacred musk was gives in the Town Hall, Frodsham, by nine members of the Wilmington Jubilee Singers, when Mr. Terme presided. Tim programs. comprised a number of those quaint, angular, and popular jubilee songs and melodiee, whieb were rendered by Mr. Davies and company in the style en peculiar to slave songs, and received the wrapt attention of the audience. The manager, Mr. Darien, gave an address illustrating the dis- advantages under which the coloured population suffer, in some parts of America, and explained that he Ira. endea- vouring to raise sufficient /nods for a mimion room to preach the Gospel to his countrymen. There ems a lair attendance, and a hearty vote of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Mr. Davies, seconded by Mr. Y. W. Dunsford, brought a pleaaant evening's entertainnaenl to a close.

Moores, Londotrread, Men- em:star, tobamooiat ; H. Swaim Pendleton Brewery, Pendle- ton ; H. Eaton, Grarenhunger, Salop, miller. roz Burrors.—At the Haat Rain? Petty , Seasions at Hull, a man, who presented a comical ap- pearance, and whose name is George Scott, alias Billy Button, was brought before the magistrates on a charge of vagrancy. The peculiarity of his appearance Ins tented by the manner in which he had aZorned his out with buttons, that garment being studded with them front top to bottom. They were of various Mee, and of all description. Though they had the look of having been rewn on indiscriminately, there appears to have been a method in which they hay, been attached. Long rows exteoded from the breast to the skirt, the whole numbering 365—the number of the days at the year. On his collar were abate a donee or more large white ones, which indicated the number of timea thetr wearer had been pat in gaol for vagrancy, and on mother part of the garment were a quantity which indicated how old he was. But this waa entail. The man had with him • bag, in which were at least four hundred more ballots, which he stated he had picked op on his travels, and with which he replaces thoee which may come off hi, coat, or add to those already no, as the exigencise of the circom stances may demand. Notwithstmding the variety of the buttons this mogulae character has with and on him, there is not one which has belonged to a police uniform, and on being asked the reason for that exception, he said be should be murdered by his companions if he were Co obtain a policeman's lotion. Stott is • native of the North of Ire- land. He was apprehended at Newingtot on Tuesday kw bemieg He appealed to the bench lobe allowed to go thio Ham, and he was let off on promising to ban* the tots.

The present Sultan and Path. of Turkey are as wily and vacillating as any of their predeueseors who have appeared on the political etage in con• section with the grieve,. Eastern Queetion. In tricks of diplomacy the Turks lave proved themselves meat. hands. A.122-iOO.B as their nsighbours may be not to re-ereate a ground for war quail every effort shall have been made to obtain hy pc t ceful twang that which would only be exacted by the employment of the breechloader, the mortar, and the sabre, ap- pearances indicate Turkey to be .till obstinate, and that she believe@ the can &till hoodwink the eivilieed world by vein promises or diplomatic ev.ioos. For 20 year. she chuckled over the eon-fulfilment of solemn promiere made on her behalf to the anembled repro- ...fives of the great Powers of Dieppe at Paris in 1866 to reform for eystem of Government in her Christian States Russia waited with impatience for the (Recharge of those obligati°ae by her Mahomme- dui neighbour, but finding that, only,, force was brought to bear upon her, than obligatioos would never be realised, the C.or appealed to the nations of Europe to join him is coercing Turkey to execute her promises The result of that appeal is too well known to need recapitulation here. Turkey became prostrate under the iron heel of Runde, and with i e oonqueror'e grip tight upon her throat Tech.>, re • sorted to her old diplomacy of making great psonises. The various Governments of Eurcpe in solemu con• dove at Berlin decreed that Turkey, . the cettagirod node, s4l old offender, ((hood submit other kingdom being partitioned. To this decisiox of the representa- tives of the European States Turkey in her day of humiliation bowed arid acquiesced. Time has rolled on, and Turkey has shown that when ette fell in with the agreement of the Power. acting in concert at Bar- lies she had not the xlight.t intsittion, utilene com- pelled—an event she deemed improbable—to carry oat the pledgee else xeriously gave; and now, when • fleet eompowd of men -of • war belonging to the chief nations of Europe are within shot moge of her coasts, waiting for a signal to shell her forts and towns, (the has had the aesurance to r.iet premiere put upon her to respect her obligations, probably ice the belief that by a further exercise of her sioompliehments in diplomatic ledgerdemaiu she can throve divisions into the councils of the nations acting in emitter; and ulti- mately baffle them out of their sense@ and ,core another victory. Am we lecorded in the Exagreimr of laet week, the threat of Mien Pooh., who is in com- mand of the Turkish regular troops in the Albanian districts, to regard any movement on the part of the Montenegrin soldier. against Duleigno as • declara- tion of war, created an altered state of affairs between the Porte and the Powers, tises, combined fleet being then of Ragusa, to lend countenanoo by ecsa to the Modeoegrins seising upon Duleigno, awarded to them by the Berlin Congress. Oliver in its eoneep• lien as this diplomatic feat wee on the part of the Sublime Porte to gain time and sow divisions among the Powere acting in edicert, . the naval com- manders of the latter had positive instructione not to give aid to the Montenegrins by lead, it further strained the relatione between the Allied Po were and the Porte, which had had the utmost forhearanoo shown to it, nod the fullest latitude allowed to fulfil its promises. The movement on the part of the Porte eonfirmed the truth of a suspicion which had been gaining ground that the Sultan's profeseion that the Abideos would resist any endeavours on hie part to hand over Dulaigno to the Montenegrin• was simply • baselees excuse. Finless that the Allied Powers, at, at least, some of the greateet of thome powers, were not see a mood to withdraw their handl( unless the decision, of the Berlin Congress were carried out by the Porte, not only so far as they affected the eaten. lion of the horde. of Montenegro but of the borders Of Greece—which has now 40,000 men in arms ready to take the field againet the Turks, nohow thdlatter ooncede the territory awarded by the Congrees—the Sultan asked to be allowed until Monday last to frame some proposals for the consideration of the Allied Powers. The propowde were contained in a note, of which conic. were handed to the Amble. .dore representing the great Powers; and it would be difficult to imagine the rulera of any etate on the brink of cliseolution submitting each self-confident and arrogant auggenione to pow°ee that were giving its loot chance to carry out its own pledgee, and who could by military and naval pro.ee speedily work its destruction, The note carries with it a tone of suppreeeed indignation that the combined squadrons should over have been sent to c.roe the Porte to soaks good her pledge to cede Duleigno to the Montenegrins., and • sort of protest against the possibility of any eueh coercion being indulged in in regard to the toonsmion of the Greek dolma the reorganisation of Armenia, and even the domestic reforms of Rounielia. The Porte proposee to do oertaiu things H the Greet Powers will disband their combined squadrons and never dare to effect such • eombinatiot in the future. One of the promisee Turkey now mak., on the conditions above named being carried out, is that she will endeavour to induce the Albanian, to surrender //deign°. If ehe cannot perthade the Albania., which she would never attempt to do if left to herself, the will withdraw her troops and not he r.po.ible for anything that may happen there. As regerds the elaime of Greece the Port is as stiff -necked as ever in its refusal to surrender the pl.es which it has already declined to give up. Indeed of adhering, it promised to do, to the frontier line mapped out by the Berlin Congr.e, it proposes alive of frontier south of Laths., and following the course of the Arta to the sea—a line which retains Janina in Turkey'. /made. This frontier line is to be ceded to Greece within one hundred dayl, in the same ruannev as in proposed for the surrender of the Duleigno district that I. to say, if Greece persists in her demand for the anion of the territory to her as awarded by the Congress, she will have to win it at the point of the .word. If Turkey had been a powerful conqueror, and had states and empires to Low to her whims and fancies, eke could hardly have sent out • Note of euch im- port ecuched in more haughty lang-usge. She calculated that by putting on a bold front she would stir up among the powers noting in ooneert all the old jealousies; and rivals, and cause the concert of Powers to end in • miserable break up and failure. But she haa overshot her reckonings for once. The line of policy eke has chceen to adopt, has, by ita insolence and arrogance, caused wroth to take the place of -.forbearance, and it has intensified the determination of the allied powers not to be baulked In their designs to have the Treaty of Berlin complied with by any clever subterfuges or smart diplomatic tricks on the part of the Porte. ToleKrains from the varioue capitol) of Enrope, except, of course, that of Turkey, comment upon the fact that the Porten note ie an I:limiting one, and will not be accepted by the . great Powers; and even in Conatantinople there is a feeling among the Pitches that the allied Powere will not submit to have such a defiant note fang into their, teeth. The Duleigno affair was but one of many matters to which the allied Powers would have had to coerce Turkey into giving iteattention, as Turkey herself woe quite aware; and unless Turkey quickly oseumee a lees defiant attitude the combined fleet, instead of covering about the Adriatic within shot Runge of the hitherto little known fort of Dedeigno, will be found within eight of the Sultan's pale,on windows at Conatatitinople. The Frenoh Goveroment, whilst willing to Iced her metal rapport to the coercion of Turkey, is prevented by tho want of the coneent of her House of Representatives, which is not sew sitting, from joining in any active hoetilitiee. The other Powers, Austria, Germany, Russia, and Italy, await the propoenis of England as to the next atep to he taken, and there is no doubt am to what that step will be. England will certainty not now withdraw from the work she has set herself to accomplish ; the Greeks will not be kept in cheek unleee her claims are satisfied; and the other great Powerr will not stand aloof from England io her work of teaching Turkey that she can no longer be permitted to be a common disturber of the peace of Europe. If the reeponsible rulers of Turkey have not taken leave of their aroma completely, they must see that nukes they conform quietly to what is demanded of them the daye of Turkish rule in Europe mast oome to an end, and that quickly. But the Porte knows how to give in to the inevitable, and ehe will devour the leek.

it. his epeech at the recent complimentary banquet give. in hie honour at St. Helens, the new Bishop of Liverpool, Dr. Ryle, expressed a hope that sotne benevolent Churchman would bake it into his head to make the munificent gift of • quarter of million of money in order that a Cathedral worthy of such • populous and wealthy diocese as that of Liverpool might be erected. The new bishops of South- well and Wakefield are in am poverty-stricken a oondition as regards majestic cathedral piles as the Bishop of Liverpool, and they find that movements which have been set on foot to raise the needful for deftaying the cost of the required strueturea make poor headway. Whether the lack of gene- rosity which this story lay. bare is doe to the want of intereat an the part of Churchmen in the projects, or whether it arises from the crippled financial condition into which the hard times have thrown all chasten of the people, it is difficult to nay. His idea in to reduce, as vacancioe occur, tha salary of the Archbishop of Cthterbory to LlO,OOO, that of his brother of York to £B,OOO, London to deteSt, Durham and Wioibcntvr to .£5,000, and the £5,000 appointments to £A,2oo—the IOrOMO thought sufficient for one of the best of tho bishops, Dr. Frame. The now thus slaved would suffice not only to support the new bishopric, but to raise Rochester, Liverpool, and Truro to .t 4,200. Our contemporary'a cor- re:pendent is evidently preparing himself to be.ome, in the future, a candiaate for the office of Chancellor of the Exchequer, where he will find abundance of cases of big salaries and pensions and little work ready prepared to his used, and awaiting such experimente as he is anxioun to apply to Rao incomes of ecclesiastical dignitaries, who rejoice in being reg trd. as the imitators and successors of the poor fishermen of Galtilee.

To anyone who was present at: the Runcorn Police Court on Monday and saw the number of mothers who were brought up before the magistrates for neglecting to mud their children to school, the eight must have “used pity for the poor unfortunate parents. IPA pity must not blind or I to the good which the Education Act is effecting through. I out the land. If the object of the Act is to be atuioed, viz, compulsory education, let. difficult., if not impoeeible, to avoid many thing. that are hard and unpleasant to those who come under its operation. I should like to tell those poor women to do their best, accept the ineritable, and not light against the School Board. When Stephenson was asked what would be the effect, if • row got on the line when oar of his steam engines was coming along, the great engineer replied, "Well, it would he bad for the coo." Those parentz who oppose the School Board will be much in in the position of that cow. I know that as regards the Run- corn School Board great forbemancehaa been exercised, and offendere hare not been prosecuted till every other resource I has folio!. Still leas should them Irate parents abuse the School El ard officer. Ile simply carries out the instructions of the Board. Ile le not a policeman, nor a detective, but generally, as in the case of the Ruecorn officer, a hard- working, pleasant-spoken gentleman, who endures wrath and often the threats of enraged parents, and who spends his mornings in courts and alleys, his afternoons in police. courts abused by magistrates, and his evening., at home doing clerk work in connection with his office. Taking one censideration with another, a School Board officer's life is net a happy one.

The entertainment entitled, "The flower queen, or the coronation of the rose," will be given in the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Wed•esday and Thursday evenings, by friends In connection with Bethnal.% Congregation Chapel. Much trouble and expense have been incurred in getting tip the affair, and as the conception of the piece in original and pleasing in Its character, it is believed that it will prove very attractive. Each of the girls or young ladies who take part in it will appear as the personification of some puticular flower, and though probably none of the dresses will be by Worth, of Paris, I have every reason to believe they will be eery pretty and attract many fair critics. The Primitive Methodists of the Preeton Brook ,irca have been very successful with their baciar. The, were not able to secure the valuable help and social influence of • gentleman like Mr. John Simian" who was prevented by the death of a relative from attending to open the hamar, but they supplied his place well with Mr. 0.8. Haslehuret, who mode a very interesting speech, MO manifested a bon- homie which charmed all who were present. Let as hope that, now that peace reigns throughout the circuit, and the finances are in • very fair condition, the friends of Primi- tive Methodiste in the circuit will experience prosperous times, and forget all about the few dark clouds which some time ago bung upon their connevional horizon. I have no doubt that there was much joy amongst the total abstainers of the district on the announcement being made by Mr. Gaglish, JP., that the Runcorn Bench of Magistrates had declined to grant the application of the licensed victuallers of Weston and Halton, that thee would recommend to the Licensing Committee that these townships ahould be placed in such • position onto keep their houses open until • later hour. Them is evidently a public senti- ment growing in favour of giving no more encouregement to public drinking, and it seems very probable that the days when a welt-rode public-boner inc fair sitna'ion could be .old for fff,ooo or £7,000 are over. It is high time. in all conscience, that the stain was wiped from our beloved I inil that ills the most drunken country on the face of theearth. The real friends of working men ought to deal 3 little less In flattery and more in unvarnished truth. It wonl,l be an advantage if one could at thnes hear lee about the n ender- (el influence of the labouring classes, and their demands for political and social rights, and • little more about time neg- lect of the common rides of prudence in regard to money shown by many of them, and their devotion to slily plea- sures which cannot boot any permanent good. Joseph Barker, the great secularist and politician, who in his later days “me back with weeping to the good old paths has written an anti-blographiml sketch, which has lately been published In one chapter of the "Teachincs of esporience"—what a stern master—he uses the following remarks, which I should be plweed to see in this column of your paper—" Aim at reforming men, rather than changing laws and institu- tions. If you enlighten and reform men, laws and institu- tions will be reformed as a matter of coarse. Laws and institutions are the work of men, and answer to- the characters of their authors. If men are wise end Food, they make arise and good laws and inetitutions t and if they are ignorant and corrupt they make foolish and miechievoualaws and institutions. We make all things in mown image, and bring down or lift up all things to oar own level. Make a people wise and good, and bad laws will first become obso- lete, wet then be abolished. Leave people ignorant and depraved, and the best laws and institutions in the world will do them little or no good. The reform of man, there- fore, is the reform of all things ; his neglect is the ruin of all things. Again be just_ and courteous, and kind to those whom you seek to reform. Give them credit for all that is true and good in their creed., character,, and cum .19. DO not be astonished or offended at their slowness to change. Good people generally change slowly, and the beat most slowly of all. Consider the power of custom, and of here- ditary tendemea; the force of education and reverence for parental authority; of men's natural and salutary distrust and dread of what I. new and untried." -;;;;I-1:177; • Vaunt, BOUND FROM Rye:cotter—A eel- lion occurred yesterday morning in the Irish Channel. The express steamer Shantrtek, from Dublin to Holyhead arrived three hours late, hartng been delayed a few milea outside the harbour through coming into collisioo with the schooner Anna, or Hannah, of C Irnarvon which WAS bound front Runcorn to Yarmouth with ult. The Shamrock ap- pears to have run Into the Anna stern on, as there were no lights viaible,end theechooner unk in two minutes after- ward.. Immediately the blow was felt and the position realited a boat wu lowered front the Shamrock to try to eafe life. The crew having rowed about for • considerable time without seeing any signs of the men belonging to the unfortunate vessel returned to the steamer, and when on the I point of heaving the boat on the davit a cry was heard some distance away. The boat wesdropped astern in the direc- tion of where the cry was heard, and In a short time enc. ceede,d in picking ups young man who formed one of the schooner's crew, and who io the only survivor. He hod managed to put himself in • cask when his rennet went down, but he found he could not manage it, and it had to be abandoned. The other three men forming the crew, in- cluding the master, Hugh Jonas, of Cunarvon, must have perished. - - .

It is Intended to devote the proceeds to the fund being raised for a minister's house. A description of the , Cantata will prove iemresting, as it is entirely new to this neighbourhood, and the music throughout is of • very charming character. The composition is from the pen of a talented American composer, Mr. ti.F. Root, of Chicago, the libretto being written by Miss PranceitJane Crosby, the blind American poet. The platform will be profusely decorated !with choice plants and flower; to give it the appearance of a dell in the forest, the fair singers being suitaldy attired, !and wearing the particular dowers they represent. A brilliant I overture commences the Cantata, and when the certain rises, !the whole of the flowers are discovered assembled in the dell to chose their Queen, this is followed by a full chorus, desoriptive of the flowers; near the close of the chorus, a distant f netstep is he.sn.l and they leave in haste. • person discontented with the world, now enters the dell, and being charmed with its beauty, expresses his desire to remain there, in the words, "There would I rest," ,kc. Ile is invited by the sound of distant voices to remain and Like up his abode. He expresses his wonder and astonishment in son& whence the sounds proceed, when two of the flowers appear, and intimate in a charming duet, that it is the music of the flowers. The flowers then re-mwernble in the dell to choose their Queen. In • number of beautiful songs each aspirant puts forth her claim to the grown. Marry uf the songs have • well arranged choral acconipaniment, prominent amongst them being the "Sunflower" which is ex- needing', effective and racy. But before the choice is concluded night comes on, mid a troop of "Poppim" enter and lull them to dorm With the subtle narcotic. A hymn dedicated to Night, by the dowers, sccon,panied in song by the Recluse, appropriately brings the first day to • close. At the break of day they again assemble, and in full chorus wish each other "Good morning." Several other !flowers then prefer their claim, after hearing which, they I appealed to the Reclu, to decide for them. Ova suitable !song he expresoes the difficulty of choosing," where natures! hand alike her gifts he.tow," but in conclusion ouggeste the "Rom "...their Queen, to which they unanimouely give their anent. Having sung the chorus "Prepare we for ! the festive scene" they return to make preparation for the : coronation. A bevy 0 litle girls then enter representing . the "Heather hells" and greet the flowers in a lively chores. The whole of the flowers, thee appear and sing • grand emanations march, eft, which four of the flowers advance to the foot of the throne, and place the coronet ow the brow of the Queen el,t, when she ascend. her ! throne, the flowers testifying their joy in the beautiful : echo chorus, "Long live our heautious Queen." The ! Recluse having expressed his intention of returning to • ! life of usefulnees and contentment, the last rind chorus, !" At the Birkenhead county magistrates' court, on Saturday, before Mr. T. It. Lee, James Clare, James Lockhart, William RusWge, Thomas Smith, James Rawson, and James Sherrard, all of Warrington, were charged with poaching at Eastham on I ind belonging to Mr. R. C. Naylor, on the night of the 24th ultimo. The first four prisoners were appreherded on the morning of the affray, and RAWSON] and , Sherrard were takvu into custody • few days ago. Mr. Moore appeared for the promcutiim, and Mr. 6herraU for the defence. The principal particulare of the calm have been already given. Mr. Moore applied for a further re- mend, stating that since the previous week the gun which had been used by the poachers had been bimmered by the police, besides thirty or forty rabbits which have been thrown into the river. The coat of one of the keepers bad , also been eaarrined bray tailor, who found in it some gun- I that holes. Ile (Mr. Moore) should prove that the prisoner. I Rawson and Sherrard formed part of the gang of poachers, I and haring done that he should ask for a remand for another week. With regard to the priminers Rawson and Sherrard he should prove an olitn. Mr. Moore then milled George Preston, a keeper on the Kenton estate, who said that shout four o'clock on the morning of the affray he wm behiod Captain !doneley (Mr. Naylot's anon, when they nme upon the poachers, who were about 20 in numbs. The poachers were pegging down a net, which was a tremendotte length, about SOO yards long. Wiles= pulled the net, when. time the prisoner struck at him. Witness then caught Rawson by the nose, when the prisoner Sherrard struck him on the shoulder. Oneself the poachers called out, "Shoot the b-- and another,. Ost with your knives, and let us go into the b—." IMMO. diately afterwards two shots were fired, and KCMGS were thrown. The fAces of all the poachers were black. Super- intendent Plant, who took the prisoner Itagrsoninto eestedv at Warrington, stated that the dewcription given by th.• keeper Preston tallied with 0 apnearance of Rawson and Sherrerd. Mr. Sherratt, for the defence, called Richard Yates and Thomas Ben-, file r h,:er., of Wartingtor, who stated that on 'Thursday night week they u ere working with the prisoner Sherrard up till half-past ten n'clo,k, nod that he (Sberrard) was against his work at Mr. &Idiom'e at half. pest six o'clock on Friday morning.—A woman named Hannah Pierpoint was called to prove that the prisoner Rawson was at home on the night of the poaching affray, The msgistrates granted a further remand of the ease till Thursday next' and consented to accept bail for the prisoners Sherrard and Broom. John Hardman, John Boardman, and Robert Leigh, who belong to a gang of well-known poacher., residing in War- rington, were charged at the Lvmm Police Court, on Thurs- day, with night poaching on Colonel Cornwall Legh's land, at High Legh, on the 9th lilt. Colonel Leith's head keeper, Meech, era. out with five other men at midnight on the 9th, when he discovered • net some 50 or OD yards long. Near the net were five or eix men, including the prisoner.. The keepers, who had some DS rabbite, put them and their nets down and ran towards the poachers, who faced the keepers, and with sticks and stones beat them off, and they had to I retreat One of the prisoners, Leigh, who had been knocked down by the keepers, was left on the field, but he wee mdse. quently rescued by his companions, who took the net. and I rabbits belonging to the keepers. Two other men concerned in the affrsy, Wm. Ratak.. anti Thomas Swift, have been committed for trial at Birkenhead, on to charge el night poaching and attempted murder at E.M.11.1111. a few nights after the affair at High Legh. div.p: MR. MeNINNIES, M.P., ON CHURCH

AND DISSENT. TV fourth and concluding lecture of the come< by the Rev. R. W. Dale, MA, of Birmingham, on " The Rice of Evangelical Noneonformity," was delivered on Townley evening, in Hope Hall, Hope-street, Liverpool, to. crowded audieuce.

McMorrows M.E., who presided, said that since they aseembled there teat week to listen to the history of early Nonconformity, there had been *erne very remarkable utterances by clergymen of the Established Church in refs ence to modern Nonconformity. (Hear, hear.) l'eehaps one of the moat remarkable of these utterantes wan by the Bishop of Lirerpool. On the whole he did not think there was much, if anything, to complain of in the tone of Bishop Ride's addreaa. His lordship was good enough to say that "English Protestant distant is • great fact—(laughter)—and it le useless to deny its exiamnce " (Renewed laughter.) Perhaps the infers.o from the great fact it was not necessary to explain. Ilia loadehip went on farther toss,—" I shall , never hesitate to deckles my conviction that in thousands of parishes dissenters have done an immense amount of , spiritual good. They have supplied the church's ' lack of , service.' They have brenght to Christ myriad. who were perishing in ignorance end sin. They have taught the elements of Christianity to multiturles who would other- wine have died without God and without hope. These are Nell which it is impossible to deny." But whiled they recognieed the kindness of Bishop Ryle in his remarks about dissenter, it was to be regretted that these marks of couramy were net universal amongst clergymen of the Church of England. On the very the and in the very town where these remarks by the Bishop of Liverpool were made, there was • meeting of clergymen and layman connected with the church, under the rangeniel presidency of Archdeacon Dension, where something very different was uttered. That we.. 'netting held to deeounce the Burials Bill, and the burden of the epeethes at that meeting seems to have been, "Come, corm me Selborne rad defy me Osborne Morgan." (Laughter.) There had been • good deal of that kind of thing since, and during the last dray or Pro we had seen in the newspapers that certain clergymen in the Church of England were deter- mined to terra, as far as they could, the operation of the Borate Act. They might have law upon their side, but certaihly they were acting against the spirit of the act, and he lied no doubt at all that if, from eome oversight, they had the law on their side, diet net was intended to open the burial yard, of this nation to the people of this nation; end if it bed failed in its object, they might depend upon it it wookl be emeeded. (Applause.) Well, at this meeting a rartain Dr. King counselled the.. present to " give the dis- senter. the cold shoulder. in the graveysed—(laughter)— for in nine canes out of ten such people had no notions at decency. (Laughter.) As tar as possible, diesenters Mould be put in one corner of the churchmant (Renewed laughter.) They should, indeed, have a special sexton, for much buriale were little else then heathen. (Loud laughter.) Another clergyman following this Dr. King seemed to have munselled soinething which the chairman himself could not tolerate, for he referred to pot the motion on the ground that it would lead to physical strife, (Laughter.) The reporters had not said precisely what fire resolution was but from the fact that the chairman thought it would Iced to physical form, he supported that If the rceointion had been carried out we shookl have seen some stalwart Baptist minister contending with same stalwart member of the Epis copal ian Church militant in their shirt sleeves at the gates of the burial ground. (Laughter.) Bishop Ryle himself was careful ho say that there wre .diseenters and dis- senters "--good diameters and had diameters. He said— "We should always remember that we must draw, broad line of distinction between dimenters and diameters. If we suppose, for example, became anme wild men are incessantly telling the public that the Fatablished Church in a Babylon which ought to be destroyed, or that all the prayer books ought to be burned, or that the union of church and rate is an adulterous connection, or that all clergymen ought to be stripped of their endowments and turned into the secrete, or that Anglican ministate are mere serfs and slaves who are paid out of the taxes—if, I say, we suppose, bemuse some dimentere talk this rabhish, that all dimentere Agree with. them, we are quite mistaken." Well now, Bishop Role mid be had known .limenters for 4(1 years Ito) Mr. McMinnits) had known dimenters a good deal longer. and he had never heard anybody say that thee would like to do all them terrible thirars againsi the Episcopalian church and clergy. (Applause.) The fact was that we were bearing sadly too much nowadays about potting down dissent and converting or abolishing dissenters. What would churchmen think if the nonconformiso were to meet, to have congresses to make mooches end to preech con. meetly on the idea that they should convert Episcopatiam aed bring them int* the fold of nonconformity. Yet this would not be one whit lees impertinent than for the mininters and laymen of the Epirarmalian Church to beeonstantly talking about bringing Dissenters into the fold of the church. Why should they attend the Episcopalian Church 1 They were quite satinfied were they were. (Applause.) Their minister, for the wont part were.. well educated, PS earnest, as useful as the minister, of the establishment. (Hear, hear.) He saw the other day what he considered rota very wise epeech by the Dean of Wraminoter, in which he mid that one of the best ways of reconciling diameters was to allow their ministers to preach in the churches of the estab- lishment. He (Mr. McMinnies) did not know, but he Dever not with a ministe amongst the Nonconformists who desired to preach in the churches of the Establishment. (Hear. heat) The only churches in the Estaboishment that thee bad any right to were for the most part very cold and comfortlme places. They had better churchot and chapele of their own, far more commodious and far more comfortable; and if they wanted any more they would build them for theme Ives. (Applautie.) And there was nothing very tempting to Nonconformists in the Episcopalim fold if they took the description of it from Episcopalians themselves. Bishop Reis in theme speech I already quoted from, said, "One own beloved Church of Ragland in infected with seeni-Romraire on the extreme , right, and semi-unhelief on the extreme left and Arch- ' ...con Denison said. "We of the church—bishops, clergy. people—are heavily to blame in this matter; we have thrown godly discipline to the winds and our retribution i• Met. The church of the future, wnich has nothing in common with the church of the par and present, is feet rasing into the room of the Church of England. and the Archbishop of Caoterbury is waiting to be Primate." He did not know what that meant it was • little incoherent : but it wen quite plain, at all events that Archdeacon Denison was not gene satisfied with what was going on in the Episcopalian Church. Considerable mieapprehension exiated as to the cause of disoent. A leading nom in the Ereblishment—he thought it waa the Bishop of Manchester—mid the other day that nonconforniity +mowing to the alarms and corruption in the church, such as the erystem of patronage and the par- ches, of church livings. There could not be a greater mis take. If what churchmen called the abuses of the church were abolished to-morrow, the nonconformists would still be dissenters on the very grounds on which their Puritan and nonconformist forefathers were dissenters They believed

that the church government of the Episcopalian denamins• tion was anscriptural. Some of them objected to the Thirty- nine Articleu on the ground of their Calvinistic tendency objected to all creeds Rod to all articles of they lelefertal more or lean with the great of the right of private ladgment in matters of J; and there ware many other matters in the liturgy of to Episcopallen Church to whish mown/smokes objected. In ...lesion, the chairman said ha did Bishop Ryle the Malice to may that he ssw that it wee utterly ion- ' parible for Indipeodents, Baptists, and Melbodiera to amalgomate with the Epimopalians; and he thought hie lordship was a wise MAU in d anointing the members of the Episcopalian Church from wasting their time in endeavour- ing te tiring about any such amalgamation. Meet- ings of the committee will be held to-day and on Monday I next, at which the report will be finallv considered. The committee will express the opinion that the Atalanta foun- dered in the terrible gale to which reference has been made in the logs of shipe which were in the track of the ill-fated vessel. THE DIFPETIENCE BETWEEN A FAiNTISO FIT AIM El,' tensy.—A fainting fit is sometimes mistaken for an Chock of epilepsy. As a rule, there is little difficulty in distinguishing between them. In epilepsy the heart beats well, and the pulse can be felt at the wrist, whilst in a faint the patient is for the moment pulseless. It is nomrtime. no easy matter to distinguish between a faint and an attack of petit mai. It must be remembered OW people do not faint without any cause, although often enough that cause is very trivial. ft may be simply the heat of the room, or long atelinence from food, bat there is always some reason.. An attack of petit nod, on the contrary, comes on momentarily and without, no fir as you can tell, an exciting cause. If any one apparently in good health is sitting quietly in in ' room not too hot, and without receiving had news or any- thing of the kind, suddenly becomes insensible, it in probably an attack of epilepsy and Bonn simple faint. If, on the other hand, the room is hot and close, the patient is del mote, and has teen excited and then suddenly becomes pale and falls, it is probably only in fainting fit.—" Vie Family rhysi.

—inn Damn OP Bali.o.—ls bread as cheap as it ought to be, considering the very low price at which wheat is gelling in the market? This question is now crmting a good deal of discussion at several great centres of industry, and from the statements made, it would almost appear that the price is considerably above what would allow a fair margin for profit. A cental-100Ihs.—of good flour, which will make from thirtv-four to thirtv-six quartern loaves, can be pur- chased at Liverpool for .froin Ifis. to Ifs. At 7d. tech, the sale of thirty-five of such loaves would bring in 201. Sal., ehowing a groan profit of le. 51. on each cental of flour , bought .1 13... the average price. This is as nearly as me- eible 50 per cent, and It therefore does appear that the bread-buying public have some came for complaint. Nor can it well be the case that the bakers give their customers the advantage of Trieste flour, which Costs les per mutt When such choice descriptions are us,.l, as they generally are in the wealthier quarters of towns, the vendor usually takes :very good care to charge a halfpenny or a penny per loaf extra. I here seems to be no reason why good, whole- some, well-baked quarters loaves, free from adulteration, should not be purchasable at fid. During last week wheat only averaged a fraction over 423. pea quarter agaimt 475. or 48s. at the same period last year, but in working.clasa localities there in little appreciable difference between the price of bread then and now. The farmere know to their ; coat that they are heavy losere by the fall In prices ; eon- I eumers are equally convinced that the fall has brought them no good ; who, then, are benefited? Public suspicion alights on the heads of bakers and millers conjointly, and credits them with being in nylon to take on the one hand instant advantage of any rise in the price of flour to enhance that of bread, mad on the other, to hold up the latter es long as pos- sible against every fall in the wheat market. Very pomibly this view of the case is somewhat exaggerated; once arouse popular suspicions and they are wont to rush into extremes. Bat the WA ilants certainly seem to hare entahlished a prima pele case against a the ring,” as they style their opponente, and it therefore rests with the latter to show that they are not victimising their customers in order to make a large pelt for themselves. Co-operative stores same into exist- ence through a trading policy of that sort, and we should not be surprised to see the system extended to bread, should the trade continue deaf to the teachings of the times. div.head: HARVEST THANKSGIVING AT ST. PA UL'S WESLEYAN CHAPEL. RUNCORN.
div.p: HARVEST THANKSGIVING AT ST. PA UL'S WESLEYAN CHAPEL. RUN- CORN.

On Sunday morning • sermon was preached in St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, by the Rev. 11. Valentine, from the text " lie reeerveth unto us the appointed semke of the harvest," dec. 5,74 In the course of his sermon Mr. Valenti.' said there was in omn,iu kis natural condition, a tendency to forget God, although in the revolutions and developmenta of nature there were such writing exhibitions of the Divine skill and power. The solution ufgne problem of all existence wee to be found in the exietence of the supreme anti Almighty God ; and yet men were to be met with ',rho re- ' Motel that mlution. They were like the Jews of This people bath •revolting and • intiellious heart they are re- volted and gone. Neither eay they to then- heart, let as now fear the Lord our God, that giveth rain, both the former end the latter, in hie season ; He reserveth unto In the ap- pointed week. of the bervera..'' tAI it not be so with them, but, as theseasons come and go. might they be led up to Hie, who mac the first end the last, the greatest and the... It yes proper just then, egged had favoured therewith theuspe pdoted weeks of the harvest," that they should take natio. 1 of his care ; and .1010th. harvest cheer wee will ringing In ' their um he would direct the., attention to the feei hags in- spired, the analogies supplied, and the lemons congested, 71 the return of that meson of the year. I. A feeling of profttend reverence should he inspired by the bountiful harvest. The world was order Divine control. Men might call it what they would—force or law—the universe was under :lie control of a Pewee •hich the atom did not emape, nor the rolling world defy. The philosophy of the little boy who said thee.,, had hem. cut out with scissors and dabbed open the sky with the thumb, was as sensible as that of those people who .crilked the worke of mature to chance. While the stars shone, the dowers bloomed, and the fields smiled. God would not be , without • witnese to His power and goodness. If they: looked at nature reverently, they would find it elevating I and inspiring. A feeling of thankfulnose and love should ! also be inspired by • contemplation ofthe harvest, which was an expression of God's wonderful beneficence. How 1 tresontly men overlooked this. Living as men, of them did in manufactoring districts they were liable to overlook the value and importance of husbandry and aviculture! pur- suit. Their harvetts were their life. 'Phankfulneris to God /Mould therefore he cultivated. There were people 1 who alwaye complained. Some people had at least one talent, but it wee • talent for grumbling. Let them be in harmony with the rest of creation, from which praise is conetantly ascending to the throne ef God. To love was grarder ihan to rule. A thankful child was better than an unthankful sage. The harvest should inspire • feeling of confidence and trust. In the abundant crops they bad proof. of God's fatherly care. and that He wills the, !leonine. and welfare of hie children. Then lived too much In dreams and reveries, anticipating troublee and trials, in- stead of implicitly trusting the Providence of God. 2 The, analogim suggested by the harvest were many and veiled. They learnt that as in nature so in motels, nothing was lost, Tho seed was sown, and aPPerentle thtown ewer. hot out of weaknesa, rorruption, and death, thereeprang strength. beauty, and life. It was so in the realm of morals and mind. niey were constantly mattering seeds which took root in the mirid,'of others. There word. might tie uttered in secret and weakness, but a resurrection was coming for all. The: eimpleet and feeblest things were productive of the greatest result.. One grain of wheat produmd thirty, sixty, or evm a hundred; and m nittaible was it that It miscalled the staff of life." It was the name in the moral world. All Gol's birth's were birth's of wmknesit whether of flower,. fruit, or oak. The Christian religion had a feeble commence- ment; the Sunday echool movement and the foreign mis- sionary enterprise likewise. Never let them despiee agencies becauie they were small. God had chosen tlme small th togs of the world to confound the mighty. As there w. • natural harvish so woold there be a moral and spiritual nee. They were ripening for the great harvent. Might they be rond grain toile gathered into the gerner with the righteous. 5. 1 bey learnt • lessen of the infallibility of the divine promises from a consideration of the subject. God had spoken to man in the (larked period of hie history, and evened him that "While the earth remaineth, meanie and harvest, cold not heat, midsummer and winter, and day and night shall nnt cease ;" and in every return of that season of the year they had a proof that God's word seas like him- self, unchangeable. .1, the Lord, change not." They learnt also the orestnem and constancy of God's goodness. The bountmu., harvest Wag not sent bemires they deserved It. but larratme God loved them. They learnt also the claims on their mrvice which harvest mercies made. They could all do itometbinr, if God's aid was invoked. It was only utiliterianiam, the blight And mildew of the present day, which gauged mon by their tank books. To enter the me' vies of tied is to eenoble the life. The commonest piecea of metal were capable of being magnetised, the smallom bits of mental lying in the field reflect the bright eunbeems, and the derkest clouds shone with splendour on the side next the sun. So, if they loved and maned God, it would odd dignity, lestre, and grandeer to their whole being. div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION,
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION,

The friends of education in Widnes are in a sLte of con- siderable excitement at present owing to the fact that the triennial election of members takes place on Saturday, the 23n1 inst. Meetings of the leading member. of the various denotninations have been held within the last few days, and rumours of various kinds fill the air. Al a Nonconformist gathering, held in Lmey-street Schoolroom. on Monday evening, Mr. Benjamin Brown presided, arid there were also present the Revs. T. Peters, C. Bingant. J. Tessvman, Messrs. Spencer, Whitby, S. Owens, G. F. Dean, Lawrenson, J H. Lea, F. H. Pankburst, T. Sadler, Shottleworth, J. Oweus, Davies, Proctor, J. Robinson, W. Sadler, Riglev, E. Smiler, C. Brown, It Fogg, and S. Robinson. Mr. S. Robin- son moved that the beet thanks of the Nonconformist voters should be given to their three representatives for the earnest attention they hot paid to the interests of the ratepayers whilat they had occupied that position. This resolution, supported by Mn. Shuttlewortb, Mr. Pankhurst, and the Chairman, was passed. It was also agreed that three can- didates should he nominated. viz., Messrs. Robert Shaw, Martin Taylor, and William Hartland, Mr. Martin Taylor h.a,ving publi:ly declined to stand, it was thought

place, should he permed in his determination. During the proceedings Mr. Taylor entered the room. and was wel.rned with a ringing cheer. He afterwerds addressed the meeting, and defended the course he had adopted whilst a member of the Board. He also stated that he deemed to retire from ,Rtce.
